sections.h2: What must a landlord do with tenant money when selling a rented house in Florida?
sections.html:
Section 83.49(7) requires the seller to hand all security deposits and advance rents to the new owner, with earned interest and an accurate accounting for each tenant account. The transfer is the landlord's job at the time of sale, so build it into the closing checklist.

Once the funds and records move and the new owner or agent signs a written receipt, the seller is released from the duty to hold that money. A new owner is presumed to have received the deposit from the previous owner, but that presumption stops at one month's rent. A buyer who skips the transfer can end up facing a tenant's refund claim for money it never saw.

Deposits have their own rules while held. The landlord keeps the money in a Florida account for the tenant's benefit, or posts a surety bond with the circuit court clerk, and must give written notice of how it is held within 30 days of receiving it. Landlords renting fewer than five units are excused from that notice, though not from holding the funds properly.

Timing at move-out matters too. A landlord who does not claim the deposit must return it within 15 days after the tenancy ends. A landlord who wants to keep part must send a written claim by certified mail or e-mail within 30 days, and the tenant then has 15 days to object. A buyer who inherits a tenancy inherits these clocks, so ask the seller for the full ledger.

  • Each tenant's deposit and advance rent amount.
  • Where the money is held and any interest earned.
  • The date each lease began and any renewal, since a renewal counts as a new rental agreement and carries the deposit forward as new.

sections.h2: Can a tenant be forced out so the house can be sold empty?
sections.html:
Only through the notices and court steps in Chapter 83. A planned sale is not on the statute's list of reasons to end a lease early, so check the lease term first and the notice period that fits it.

Section 83.57 sets the notice to end a periodic tenancy, measured before the end of the rental period.

  • Month to month: not less than 30 days' notice.
  • Year to year: not less than 60 days' notice.
  • Quarter to quarter: not less than 30 days' notice.
  • Week to week: not less than 7 days' notice.

A tenant with a fixed-term lease generally stays through the term unless the lease or the statute provides a ground to end it. Ask a Florida landlord-tenant attorney about your lease language before promising a buyer an empty house.

sections.h2: What notices apply if the tenant is behind or breaking the lease?
sections.html:
Nonpayment gets a 3-day notice under section 83.56(3), counted without Saturdays, Sundays or court-observed holidays. The notice demands the rent or possession.

Other violations are split into two kinds. For a curable violation, the tenant has 7 days after delivery to fix it. For an incurable one, such as intentional damage to the property or continued unreasonable disturbance, the notice gives 7 days to vacate. A repeat of the same violation within 12 months lets the landlord sue without new notice.

Delivery can be by mail, handing over a true copy, e-mail under section 83.505, or leaving a copy at the residence when the tenant is absent. A lease cannot waive these notice requirements. If the landlord accepts partial rent after serving a 3-day notice, the landlord must give a receipt with the balance due, pay that rent into the court registry when filing, or serve a new notice.

sections.h2: How does an eviction case move once the notice period ends?
sections.html:
The landlord files suit, the tenant has a short window to answer with rent in the registry, and a sheriff enforces any judgment.

Under section 83.60(2), a tenant who raises any defense other than payment must pay accrued rent into the court registry, or file a motion to determine rent, within 5 days after service, again excluding Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays. If the tenant does not, the defenses are waived and the landlord gets an immediate default judgment.

After judgment, the clerk issues a writ to the sheriff, who puts the landlord back in possession after 24 hours' conspicuously posted notice. Under section 83.62 weekends and holidays do not stop that 24-hour clock. A sale timeline should leave room for each of these steps, since none of them can be skipped.

sections.h2: What does the landlord owe the tenant before and after the sale?
sections.html:
The landlord must disclose in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, the name and address of the landlord or the person authorized to receive notices and demands. Section 83.50 says that person keeps the authority until the tenant is told otherwise.

After a sale, tenants need to know where to send rent and notices. Send a written notice of the new owner's or agent's name and address, delivered to the tenant's residence or by e-mail under section 83.505. This is a practical reading of the disclosure rule, so confirm the wording with your closing attorney.

sections.h2: What taxes and costs should a landlord-seller expect?
sections.html:
The sale deed carries documentary stamp tax at 70 cents per $100 of consideration under section 201.02, paid to the clerk when the deed is recorded. All parties to the document are liable for it, whoever agrees to pay.

A rental house is not homestead, so it has no Save Our Homes cap. Non-homestead assessed value can rise by no more than 10 percent a year, and the buyer's year-one assessment resets to just value after a change of ownership. Tax bills go out in November with the early-payment discount of 4 percent in November, 3 percent in December, 2 percent in January and 1 percent in February, and unpaid taxes become delinquent April 1.

If the house was rented out after being the owner's home, the homestead exemption ends when it is rented. Ask the county property appraiser to remove it and the tax collector what is owed before closing.

faqs.q: What happens to my tenant's security deposit when I sell?
faqs.a: Transfer it. Section 83.49(7) requires the seller to pass the deposits and advance rents to the new owner with earned interest and an accounting for each tenant. Get a written receipt, and the seller is released from holding the money.

faqs.q: How much notice do I give a month-to-month tenant?
faqs.a: At least 30 days before the end of a monthly period under section 83.57. Year-to-year tenancies need 60 days, quarter-to-quarter 30 days and week-to-week 7 days.

faqs.q: Can I evict a tenant just because I am selling?
faqs.a: Not on that ground alone. You need a legal basis from Chapter 83, such as a properly served nonpayment or violation notice or the end of a periodic tenancy. Check your lease term with a Florida attorney.

faqs.q: How long does the 3-day notice for unpaid rent last?
faqs.a: Three days, not counting Saturdays, Sundays or court-observed legal holidays, under section 83.56(3). It demands payment or possession and can be delivered by mail, hand, e-mail or posting at the home if the tenant is absent.

faqs.q: Who tells the tenant where to send rent after a sale?
faqs.a: The landlord, or the person authorized to receive notices, must tell the tenant in writing who to contact. Section 83.50 keeps that authorization in place until the tenant is told otherwise, so send a new-owner notice at closing.
